text: Write a program showing that a method cannot change its caller's variable, even for an object, unless it mutates through the reference. Fill in the three blanks.
choices: static void reassign(int[] arr) { ___; }   // point the parameter elsewhere
static void mutate(int[] arr)   { ___; }   // change what it points at
explanation: Verified: [1] then [99]. Java is pass-by-value always — what is copied is the reference, so reassigning the parameter rebinds a local copy and the caller sees nothing, while writing through it reaches the shared object. "Java passes objects by reference" is a common summary and it is wrong in a way that predicts the wrong answer for the first method. Chapter 12 gives the stack-frame account of why.
